newsitem.title: USA: Kids rate the season's newest toys.
newsitem.headline: Kids rate the season's newest toys.

text.p: When it comes to rating the season's newest toys, who better to ask than kids?
A group of children recently gave the thumbs up -- and thumbs down -- to a wide range of toys, and reported their findings in the November/December issue of Zillions, Consumer Reports for Kids.
More than half of the 10 new toys tested by the group of 31 kids were rated either very good or good on the fun meter.
They are:

-- Brain Warp (Tiger Electronics, 5 years and over, $25). Flip the toy to the right colour to test memory and the ability to figure out secret codes. Testers said the toy was challenging and one said, "you never get tired of it." Score: very good

-- Power Zone (Tyco, ages 8 and up, $50). Load discs into a swiveling shooter, then aim and fire them so they skid across the space-station arena. One tester said, "it's fast paced and never gets boring." Score: very good.

-- Koosh Skoops (IddzOn Products, ages 4 and up, $15). Play catch with a Koosh ball and two wide-mouthed scoops. Most testers needed some practice but after getting the hang of it, one called it "a fun twist on plain old catch." Score: good.

-- Cold Turkey (Milton Bradley, ages 4 and up, $18). Try to get the plastic "ice cubes" back on the "cold turkey." Some testers were sceptical but one said after playing, "it's an excellent game to practice your reflexes." Score: good.

-- Nerf Max Force Manta Ray (Kenner, ages 7 and up, $20). Load up the Manta Ray shield with sucker darts and fire at your opponent. Players called the Manta Ray "one of the best Nerf toys ever made." But the price only buys one shooter and to really have fun, your opponent needs one as well. Score: good.

-- Jet Turbo Samurai (Tyco. Ages 8 and up. $60). Use a transmitter to control the radio-controlled motorcycle. Some kids said it was fun to make the cycle do tricks and go in circles but others found it hard to control. Score: good.
The testers found the remaining three toys either fair or poor and gave a warning to avoid one. These toys are:

-- Nick & Nerf Dizzy Dodge-ball (Kenner, ages 6 and up, $15). Two players slip on the wrist straps of the elasticised cord and yank the cord to control the ball and play dodge-ball games. Some kids found it overpriced and one-on-one dodge-ball "is hard, and it's endless," a tester said. Score: fair.
-- Air Jammer (Ohio Art, ages 5 and up, $16.50). Launch the basketball player figure and see if he makes a basket. "It was a good idea" that didn't score, a tester said. Score: poor.

-- Dueling Racers (K'Nex, ages 7 and up, $15). The K'Nex set builds two race cars with spring-powered motors. "The building part was fun," one kid said, but most agreed that once the cares were built they moved very slowly and quickly became boring. Score: poor.

The Zillions toy testers gave a warning to Wild Planet Toy's Supersonic Ear ($19). This listening device, designed to pick up sounds from birds, insects and the like, has no volume control and makes some sounds too loud. Zillions said, "We think this toy is too dangerous for anyone's ears."
Avery Dennison, the office products company, has developed a product that helps kids make their own stickers, signs and even "kid business cards."
Avery Kids' Printertainment Software and Supplies brings this "virtual print shop" to life for kids aged 4 to 13.
The product includes a Printertainment Software Kit, which is an IBM-compatible, CD-Rom starter kit. The kit also includes one sheet of several different stickers and cards. It costs about $24.99
A package of 10 sheets of stickers or five sheets of laminated business cards costs $8.99 each.
Avery Denison, based in Diamond Bar, Calif., said the products should be available within a month in computer and office supply stores and mass market retailers.
